claims.claim: Small model + strict JSON schema + batching cuts unit cost by >80%
claims.measured: Sonnet write-up → Haiku schema -99.4%. Where it comes from: asking for the classification instead of a write-up -90.2% (Sonnet) / -88.4% (Haiku); Sonnet → Haiku -95.0% (same JSON task); the JSON schema itself +30.4% / +29.8% over the same classification asked as plain text; Batch API −50% (computed, not run: $0.094/1k)
claims.note: The >80% holds for the bundle, but not for the reason the claim gives: the saving comes from asking for the classification instead of a write-up and from the smaller model; the schema raises cost and changes no answer. What it buys is a guaranteed format (all 72 plain-text classification answers were readable here; the reader model read 100/100 fields of JSON answers rewritten as text back correctly). Batching was priced, not run. Write-ups now run at max_tokens 8,192 and none was cut off, so the baseline is no longer a lower bound.

claims.measured: same classification task, fields correct of 126: Sonnet schema 126, Haiku schema 120 (90–98%), Gemini 123; items fully correct of 36: 36 / 33 / 33. Write-ups, reported separately as usability: 69 / 69 of 126 fields usable as a classification (Sonnet / Haiku)
claims.note: Like for like (the same fields asked of both versions), the Haiku schema version matched 6 fewer of 126 fields than the Sonnet schema version (−4.8 points), all on 2 tickets (tkt-01, tkt-02); the 95% Wilson intervals overlap. The Gemini version's contains_pii did not match on tkt-05 in 3 of 3 runs. The write-up prompt never lists the allowed labels, so a write-up's score measures whether one allowed label can be read off it, not the rest of the write-up's content; it is not compared with the classification scores. Free text was read by a blind reader model (`claude-opus-5-5`, one pass). Implicit-row rule: no clear loss is detected (the intervals overlap), but the point estimates are lower and 36 runs cannot exclude a loss.

claims.claim: Section templates + length bounds control output cost
claims.measured: same model (Sonnet): −54%; + Haiku: −98%; 1-section regen vs full re-draft: −49%
claims.note: The cost claim holds, but the saving is not free: graded blind, the templated drafts score lower on accuracy (3.92 → 3.08 / 2.58) and have more serious errors (1 → 6 / 10); see the quality table and the implicit-claim row.

claims.measured: head-to-head: templated drafts preferred over the unbounded draft in 0/16 comparisons (0 ties; 95% Wilson 0–19%); accuracy 3.92 unbounded vs 3.08 / 2.58 (Sonnet / Haiku template), coverage 4.92 vs 4.00 / 3.50; serious errors 1 vs 6 / 10. Not worse: core facts 32/32 vs 32/32 / 32/32. Better: clarity 4.00 vs 4.92 / 4.42, concision 2.83 vs 4.17 / 4.08
claims.note: Blind LLM judge (`claude-opus-5-5`, not one of the models under test; 3 rubric passes per draft; every pair shown in both orders, position-consistent in 11/12 pairs), one draft per rung × 4 documents; the lead verified the serious errors against the source payloads. Shorter drafts keep every core fact and read better, but they are less accurate and less complete and lose every head-to-head comparison. The template requires an owner and a time window for every action item; the grader flagged an owner or deadline the source does not support in 16 of 24 templated action items (12 with a serious error). A single judge may favour longer drafts (its prompt tells it to ignore length and layout), but the serious errors were verified against the sources, so they do not rest on the judge's taste. Follow-up (not the app's template): one added sentence letting the template write "Not stated in source" cut serious errors per draft from 1.25 / 2.25 to 0.00 / 0.25 (Sonnet / Haiku, 12 fresh drafts each) and raised accuracy from 3.25 / 2.67 to 4.17 / 3.83, but actionability fell (3.67 / 3.25 → 3.08 / 2.67) and the long draft is still preferred in 15 of 16 comparisons. This row grades the template as the app ships it. Implicit-row rule: a clear loss (the head-to-head record is one-sided).

claims.claim: Pair hybrid retrieval (reranking + chunk filtering) with context caching
claims.measured: paired rung (Haiku picks 5 clauses from the cached full corpus, Sonnet answers over them; current answer format; n=24 per corpus size): expected clauses kept 99% / 99% (7 / 21 documents) vs BM25+rerank 100% / 87%; other suppliers' clauses selected 0/120 vs 24/120; $/question billed $0.0230 / $0.0250 vs BM25+rerank $0.0234 / $0.0262 and cached full corpus $0.0253 / $0.0379; grader correctness 4.75 / 4.54 vs cached full corpus 4.96 / 4.83; answers with a serious error 0/24 / 2/24 vs 0/24 / 0/24; before the 2026-11-26 answer-format change (original instructions, separate sessions): correctness 4.54 / 4.38, answers with a serious error 1/24 / 6/24
claims.note: Rule (current answer format, both corpus sizes; "clearly" = 95% Wilson intervals do not overlap): retrieval holds if the paired rung's share of expected clauses kept is not clearly lower, and its share of other-supplier clauses selected not clearly higher, than BM25+rerank's; cost holds if it is cheaper per question billed than BM25+rerank in 8-question sessions; quality holds if its share of answers with a serious error is not clearly higher (95% Wilson intervals do not overlap) than the cached full corpus at the same size. Retrieval holds; cost holds; quality holds, although grader correctness is still below the cached full corpus (4.75 / 4.54 vs 4.96 / 4.83). Warm, the cached full corpus is cheaper per question; it overtakes the paired rung once 13 (7 documents) / 30 (21 documents) questions share one cache write. The same rule applied to the original-format sessions gives SUPPORTED (serious errors 1/24 / 6/24 vs 0/24 / 0/24). So the move from this row's earlier PARTLY verdict, which was set by hand on the lower correctness and the claims that the documents lack terms they contain, comes from applying the written rule, not from the answer-format change; the change removed those claims and cut the serious errors.

claims.measured: answers with a serious error (7 / 21 documents, n=24 each; current answer formats): naive 1/24 / 3/24, cached full corpus 0/24 / 0/24, BM25+rerank 2/24 / 3/24 (before: 0/24 / 8/24, correctness 4.71 / 3.96), paired 0/24 / 2/24 (before: 1/24 / 6/24, correctness 4.54 / 4.38); grader correctness naive 4.50 / 4.50, cached 4.96 / 4.83, BM25+rerank 4.54 / 4.33, paired 4.75 / 4.54; key facts BM25+rerank 150/159 / 144/159 vs cached 150/159 / 149/159
claims.note: Clear loss: a version's share of answers with a serious error is clearly higher (95% Wilson intervals do not overlap) than the version it replaces at the same corpus size (retrieval vs the cached full corpus; caching vs the naive full corpus); each version in its current answer format. Caching the full corpus loses nothing (it has the fewest serious errors at both sizes). Retrieval loses nothing by this rule at either size. Before the retrieval versions' 2026-11-26 answer-format change it did: BM25+rerank at 21 docs (8/24) vs the cached full corpus's 0/24. Grader correctness on the retrieval versions is still below the cached full corpus at 21 documents (4.33 and 4.54 vs 4.83). Implicit-row rule: no clear loss is detected, but point estimates are lower (the cached full corpus vs naive at 7 docs: key facts 150/159 vs 156/159; the cached full corpus vs naive at 21 docs: key facts 149/159 vs 150/159; BM25+rerank vs the cached full corpus at 7 docs: serious errors 2/24 vs 0/24, correctness 4.54 vs 4.96; BM25+rerank vs the cached full corpus at 21 docs: serious errors 3/24 vs 0/24, correctness 4.33 vs 4.83, key facts 144/159 vs 149/159; the paired rung vs the cached full corpus at 7 docs: correctness 4.75 vs 4.96; the paired rung vs the cached full corpus at 21 docs: serious errors 2/24 vs 0/24, correctness 4.54 vs 4.83), and 24 answers per cell cannot show the versions are equal, so the row is PARTLY. Before and after are separate session sets; the change was measured on the retrieval versions only. Blind grader, one pass per answer; the deterministic key facts move less than the grader's error count.

claims.claim: Max-step budgets + deterministic guardrails + small-model routing for routine tool calls
claims.measured: max-step budgets: never bound — 0 of 198 runs hit a cap; versions with a 12-turn safety cap finished in at most 4 turns, the policy-tool versions in 4 of 5; deterministic guardrails (policy tool on the narrow-query Sonnet version): cost +18% billed ($43.10 → $50.84/1k), turns 3.0 → 4.0, exact vouchers 33/33 → 33/33; on inv-06, where the tool is wrong, 6/6 gated runs committed its figures and 0/6 matched the manual, vs 12/12 without it; small-model routing: Haiku instead of Sonnet on the narrow query -94% billed ($43.10 → $2.40/1k), exact 33/33 → 33/33; with the policy tool, Haiku-first + escalation -56% vs gated Sonnet (escalated 15/33)
claims.note: Judged in three parts. (1) Step budgets: not shown — no loop ran long on these invoices, so a budget saved nothing here; whether it prevents runaway cost is untested. (2) Deterministic guardrails: not supported — the policy gate changed cost +18% and turns 3.0 → 4.0, exact vouchers 33 → 33 of 33; on the invoice where its rule is wrong the committed voucher carried the tool's figures in 6 of 6 gated runs, as that version's instructions require, while 12 of 12 runs without it matched the manual. (3) Small-model routing: supported — switching to the small model changed cost -94% with exact vouchers 33 → 33 of 33. The saving across the ladder comes from the narrow query (-61%) and the model choice. As a whole: 1 of 3 levers supported, 1 contradicted, 1 never came into play.

claims.measured: exact vouchers (n=33 each): Raw tables, Sonnet, no cache (app rung 1) 33/33; Raw tables, Sonnet, cached manual 32/33; Narrow query, Sonnet, cached 33/33; Narrow query + policy gate, Sonnet (app rung 2) 33/33; Narrow query, Haiku, cached 33/33; Narrow query + policy gate, Haiku → Sonnet on escalation (app rung 3) 33/33; on inv-06 (policy tool wrong): without the tool 12/12 correct, with it 0/6
claims.note: Rule: a lever loses accuracy when its exact-voucher rate is clearly lower (95% Wilson intervals do not overlap). Pooled, every version scored 32/33 or better and no interval separates, so no loss is detected; at this ceiling small differences cannot be detected either. The policy tool does lose accuracy where its rule disagrees with the manual: its intervals on that invoice do not overlap with the no-tool runs'. The invoices test simple arithmetic. Implicit-row rule: no clear loss pooled; the reference version is at the ceiling, so a loss cannot be detected; and the loss on that one invoice keeps the row at PARTLY.

claims.claim: Isolate sub-agent contexts, cache the shared repo prefix, measure cost per verified outcome (CpO)
claims.measured: CpO per verified fix: Shared bus, original instructions $0.696 (15/15 verified); Shared bus, matched instructions + gate $0.469 (15/15 verified); Isolated + cached repo prefix + gate $0.100 (15/15 verified); Tiered: Haiku agents + Sonnet patch author $0.056 (15/15 verified)
claims.note: Cost per verified fix falls ~12× from the shared bus to the tiered swarm (isolation + caching alone, same instructions: $0.469 → $0.100), while the verified rate is the same in every arm. The tasks are too easy to show a quality effect (ceiling): every saving is cost per run, and CpO adds nothing over it here, so the outcome side of the claim is untested.
